generalizedRange: Sahelian grasslands of central Chad (reintroduced); formerly North Africa
hook: Extinct in the wild by 2000. By 2023, six hundred ran free in Chad.

story.text: Both sexes carry the horns that name it — ridged, sharp-tipped, several feet long, curved back like a scimitar.
It grazes by night, lets its body temperature climb to 116°F, and goes months, even years, without drinking.
Hundreds of thousands once ranged the grasslands fringing the Sahara, in herds that swelled past a thousand on migration.
Hunting, armed by the vehicles and weapons of World War II, emptied that range; the last wild photograph was taken in Niger in 1980.
By the late 1980s the last were gone from Chad; in 2000 the IUCN declared it Extinct in the Wild.
It survived in zoos — Marwell has kept it since 1972 — and in Abu Dhabi's world herd, now over 4,000.
In 2016 the first oryx flew from Abu Dhabi to Chad's Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim reserve, each wearing a satellite collar; the first wild calf came that December.
Since then 285 have been released and 510 calves born wild; by 2023 the herd passed 600, survival above 85 percent.
On 11 December 2023 the IUCN moved it from Extinct in the Wild to Endangered — the fourth large mammal returned to the wild in a century.
To witness the scimitar-horned oryx is to stand with the ecoguards, communities and scientists of central Chad keeping a returned animal wild.

reproduction.text: A single calf of about 22 pounds is born after eight to eight-and-a-half months; in Chad, 510 calves have been born wild since the first release in 2016.

insight.text: An oryx can go months, even years, without drinking — and lets its body temperature climb to 116°F rather than sweat the water away.
